export interface QuizQuestion {
  id: string;
  question: string;
  answers: { id: string; text: string }[];
  correctAnswer: string;
  reward: number;
  successMessage: string;
  retryMessage: string;
  category: string;
}

export const quizQuestions: QuizQuestion[] = [
  // ── Foundations ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  {
    id: "inflation-basics",
    question: "What does inflation mean?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "Money buys more over time" },
      { id: "B", text: "Money loses purchasing power over time" },
      { id: "C", text: "Banks give out free money" },
      { id: "D", text: "Prices always go down" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "B",
    reward: 25,
    successMessage: "Inflation is the silent enemy of unmanaged cash. +25 points!",
    retryMessage: "Inflation = money loses purchasing power. The same amount buys less over time.",
    category: "Inflation",
  },
  {
    id: "emergency-fund",
    question: "How many months of expenses should an emergency fund cover?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "1 week" },
      { id: "B", text: "1 month" },
      { id: "C", text: "3–6 months" },
      { id: "D", text: "10 years" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "C",
    reward: 25,
    successMessage: "3–6 months is the safe cushion for income loss or unexpected expenses. +25 points!",
    retryMessage: "The goal is 3–6 months of essential expenses — realistic protection against most surprises.",
    category: "Emergency Fund",
  },
  {
    "id": "saving-habit",
    "question": "Which transfer is safe when income varies?",
    "answers": [
      {
        "id": "A",
        "text": "Save a fixed amount even if bills are unpaid"
      },
      {
        "id": "B",
        "text": "Borrow money to keep saving every month"
      },
      {
        "id": "C",
        "text": "Choose an affordable amount after essentials and minimum payments"
      },
      {
        "id": "D",
        "text": "Transfer all income before checking upcoming bills"
      }
    ],
    "correctAnswer": "C",
    "reward": 25,
    "successMessage": "An optional transfer uses affordable surplus after essentials and required minimum payments. +25 local points.",
    "retryMessage": "Reserve essentials and required minimum payments first. Then choose an optional transfer from available surplus. Recheck its amount and timing when income varies; pause when there is no surplus.",
    "category": "Saving Habit"
  },
  {
    id: "interest-rates",
    question: "What happens to your variable-rate loan when the central bank raises interest rates?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "Your monthly payments go down" },
      { id: "B", text: "Nothing changes — fixed rates only" },
      { id: "C", text: "Your monthly payments go up" },
      { id: "D", text: "The loan is automatically refinanced" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "C",
    reward: 25,
    successMessage: "Variable-rate loans track the benchmark rate. When central banks raise rates, your payments rise. +25 points!",
    retryMessage: "Variable-rate loans are tied to benchmark rates. When rates rise, so do your monthly payments.",
    category: "Credit & Rates",
  },

  // ── Money Mindset ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  {
    id: "net-worth",
    question: "What is 'net worth'?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "Your monthly salary after tax" },
      { id: "B", text: "Total assets minus total liabilities" },
      { id: "C", text: "How much cash you have in your wallet" },
      { id: "D", text: "Your credit score" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "B",
    reward: 25,
    successMessage: "Net worth = assets minus liabilities at the same date. It describes a financial position, not your value as a person or whether cash is available for this month's bills. +25 points!",
    retryMessage: "Net worth is assets minus liabilities at the same date. Income is a flow; cash and credit scores are different measures. Net worth alone does not describe liquidity or your value as a person.",
    category: "Money Mindset",
  },
  {
    id: "lifestyle-inflation",
    question: "What is 'lifestyle inflation'?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "Government increasing minimum wage" },
      { id: "B", text: "Prices rising faster than salaries" },
      { id: "C", text: "Choosing more discretionary spending as your income rises" },
      { id: "D", text: "Inflating your lifestyle on your resume" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "C",
    reward: 25,
    successMessage: "Lifestyle inflation concerns choices about a higher standard of living. Higher prices or necessary costs are different. If there is a surplus after needs and commitments, you can choose to save part of it. +25 points!",
    retryMessage: "Lifestyle inflation is a voluntary rise in discretionary spending as income grows. It is different from price inflation or necessary expenses, and it does not mean every raise is fully spent.",
    category: "Money Mindset",
  },
  {
    id: "pay-yourself-first",
    question: "What does 'pay yourself first' mean?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "Spend on yourself before paying bills" },
      { id: "B", text: "Plan affordable savings after reserving money for essentials and required minimum payments" },
      { id: "C", text: "Increase your own salary first" },
      { id: "D", text: "Buy luxury items before groceries" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "B",
    reward: 20,
    successMessage: "Plan savings from available surplus after protecting essentials and required minimum payments. With irregular income, review each payment; with no surplus, skip the transfer. +20 points!",
    retryMessage: "First reserve money for essentials and required minimum payments, then choose savings from available surplus before discretionary spending. A transfer is optional; no surplus means no transfer, without blame.",
    category: "Money Mindset",
  },

  // ── Saving Habit ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  {
    "id": "budget-50-30-20",
    "question": "With PLN 4,000 take-home income, what is the illustrative 20% bucket?",
    "answers": [
      {
        "id": "A",
        "text": "PLN 1,200"
      },
      {
        "id": "B",
        "text": "PLN 800"
      },
      {
        "id": "C",
        "text": "PLN 2,000"
      },
      {
        "id": "D",
        "text": "PLN 4,000"
      }
    ],
    "correctAnswer": "B",
    "reward": 25,
    "successMessage": "20% of PLN 4,000 is PLN 800. The percentages are a flexible guide. +25 local points.",
    "retryMessage": "4,000 × 20% = PLN 800. In this example, required minimum debt payments are included once in needs; the 20% bucket is savings and extra debt repayment. This is our illustration convention, not a compulsory split.",
    "category": "Saving Habit"
  },
  {
    "id": "high-yield-savings",
    "question": "Which checklist is most complete when comparing savings accounts in Poland?",
    "answers": [
      {
        "id": "A",
        "text": "Only the advertised interest rate"
      },
      {
        "id": "B",
        "text": "Rates and conditions, fees, access, and deposit protection"
      },
      {
        "id": "C",
        "text": "Whether the account guarantees an inflation-beating return"
      },
      {
        "id": "D",
        "text": "Whether your deposit is automatically invested in stocks"
      }
    ],
    "correctAnswer": "B",
    "reward": 20,
    "successMessage": "Compare actual conditions and costs, not just the advertised rate. +20 local points.",
    "retryMessage": "Check the rate and its duration, qualifying conditions, fees, withdrawal access, and the applicable deposit guarantee scheme. A deposit account is not a stock investment; inflation can still reduce purchasing power.",
    "category": "Saving Habit"
  },
  {
    "id": "dca",
    "question": "You invest PLN 100 twice, at PLN 10 then PLN 20 per unit. What do you buy?",
    "answers": [
      {
        "id": "A",
        "text": "10 units both times"
      },
      {
        "id": "B",
        "text": "5 units then 10 units"
      },
      {
        "id": "C",
        "text": "10 units then 5 units"
      },
      {
        "id": "D",
        "text": "A guaranteed profit"
      }
    ],
    "correctAnswer": "C",
    "reward": 30,
    "successMessage": "The same PLN 100 buys 10 units, then 5 units. DCA can still lose money. +30 local points.",
    "retryMessage": "100 ÷ 10 = 10 units; 100 ÷ 20 = 5 units. DCA uses equal amounts at regular intervals, not equal unit counts. At PLN 8 per unit, all 15 units are worth PLN 120 against PLN 200 invested: a PLN 80 loss, ignoring fees and taxes.",
    "category": "Saving Habit"
  },

  // ── Inflation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  {
    id: "real-return",
    question: "What is the real return on your savings if inflation is 5% and your bank gives 2%?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "+7%" },
      { id: "B", text: "+2%" },
      { id: "C", text: "0%" },
      { id: "D", text: "−3%" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "D",
    reward: 30,
    successMessage: "Real return = nominal rate − inflation = 2% − 5% = −3%. Your money loses purchasing power even in a savings account. +30 points!",
    retryMessage: "Real return = nominal rate − inflation rate. 2% − 5% = −3%. You're losing ground.",
    category: "Inflation",
  },
  {
    id: "rule-of-72",
    question: "What is the 'rule of 72'?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "You need 72 months to pay off any debt" },
      { id: "B", text: "Divide 72 by annual return rate to estimate years to double your money" },
      { id: "C", text: "Save 72% of your income" },
      { id: "D", text: "Retire at 72 to maximize pension" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "B",
    reward: 30,
    successMessage: "72 ÷ annual return % = years to double your money. At 8%, money doubles in ~9 years. +30 points!",
    retryMessage: "Rule of 72: 72 ÷ return rate = years to double your money. Mental shortcut for compound growth.",
    category: "Inflation",
  },
  {
    id: "inflation-hedge",
    question: "Which is considered the best long-term hedge against inflation?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "Keeping cash under the mattress" },
      { id: "B", text: "Savings account at 1%" },
      { id: "C", text: "Broad equity index funds (stocks)" },
      { id: "D", text: "Lottery tickets" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "C",
    reward: 25,
    successMessage: "Broadly diversified stock index funds have historically outpaced inflation over the long term. +25 points!",
    retryMessage: "Broad equity index funds have historically beaten inflation over 10+ year horizons.",
    category: "Inflation",
  },

  // ── Credit & Rates ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  {
    id: "debt-avalanche",
    question: "What is the 'debt avalanche' strategy?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "Taking new loans to pay old loans" },
      { id: "B", text: "Paying off smallest debts first regardless of interest rate" },
      { id: "C", text: "Paying off highest-interest debts first to minimize total interest" },
      { id: "D", text: "Ignoring debt until it grows" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "C",
    reward: 30,
    successMessage: "Debt avalanche = attack highest interest rate first. Saves the most money mathematically. +30 points!",
    retryMessage: "Debt avalanche: pay off highest-interest debt first. Saves the most money overall.",
    category: "Credit & Rates",
  },
  {
    id: "credit-score-factors",
    question: "Which factor has the BIGGEST impact on your credit score?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "Number of credit cards you own" },
      { id: "B", text: "Payment history (paying on time)" },
      { id: "C", text: "Age of your oldest account" },
      { id: "D", text: "Your income level" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "B",
    reward: 25,
    successMessage: "Payment history is ~35% of your credit score — the single biggest factor. Always pay on time. +25 points!",
    retryMessage: "Payment history accounts for ~35% of a credit score. Paying on time, every time, is the #1 driver.",
    category: "Credit & Rates",
  },
  {
    id: "bond-prices",
    question: "What happens to bond prices when interest rates rise?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "Bond prices rise" },
      { id: "B", text: "Bond prices fall" },
      { id: "C", text: "No change" },
      { id: "D", text: "Bond prices double" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "B",
    reward: 30,
    successMessage: "Bonds and interest rates move inversely. When rates rise, existing bonds become less attractive → prices fall. +30 points!",
    retryMessage: "Bonds and interest rates are inversely related: rates up → bond prices down.",
    category: "Credit & Rates",
  },

  // ── Emergency Fund ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  {
    id: "emergency-fund-characteristics",
    question: "Which is NOT a characteristic of a good emergency fund?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "Easily accessible (liquid)" },
      { id: "B", text: "Covers 3–6 months of expenses" },
      { id: "C", text: "Invested in high-risk stocks for maximum growth" },
      { id: "D", text: "Kept separate from everyday spending account" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "C",
    reward: 25,
    successMessage: "Emergency fund = liquid and safe, NOT invested in volatile assets. Accessibility matters most. +25 points!",
    retryMessage: "An emergency fund must be liquid and low-risk. High-risk stocks defeat the purpose.",
    category: "Emergency Fund",
  },
  {
    id: "emergency-fund-start",
    question: "If 3–6 months seems too hard, what is the recommended first milestone?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "$10,000 regardless of expenses" },
      { id: "B", text: "One month of essential expenses" },
      { id: "C", text: "Three credit card limits" },
      { id: "D", text: "50% of annual salary" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "B",
    reward: 20,
    successMessage: "Start with 1 month. That alone covers most common emergencies. Build from there. +20 points!",
    retryMessage: "One month of essential expenses is the first realistic milestone for an emergency fund.",
    category: "Emergency Fund",
  },

  // ── Long-Term Investing ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
  {
    id: "compound-interest",
    question: "What is compound interest?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "Interest paid only on the original amount" },
      { id: "B", text: "A bank fee for early withdrawal" },
      { id: "C", text: "Interest earned on both principal and previously earned interest" },
      { id: "D", text: "Interest you pay on credit cards only" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "C",
    reward: 30,
    successMessage: "Compound interest = earning interest on your interest. Over time it creates exponential growth. +30 points!",
    retryMessage: "Compound interest: you earn interest on your interest — creates exponential growth over time.",
    category: "Long-Term Investing",
  },
  {
    id: "diversification",
    question: "What does 'diversification' mean in investing?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "Putting all your money in one strong stock" },
      { id: "B", text: "Spreading investments across different assets to reduce risk" },
      { id: "C", text: "Investing only in government bonds" },
      { id: "D", text: "Changing your portfolio every week" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "B",
    reward: 25,
    successMessage: "Don't put all your eggs in one basket. Diversification reduces the risk of one bad investment ruining your portfolio. +25 points!",
    retryMessage: "Diversification = spreading money across different assets to reduce risk.",
    category: "Long-Term Investing",
  },
  {
    id: "index-fund",
    question: "Which type of fund tracks a market index automatically with low fees?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "Hedge fund" },
      { id: "B", text: "Index fund / ETF" },
      { id: "C", text: "Venture capital fund" },
      { id: "D", text: "Pension fund" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "B",
    reward: 25,
    successMessage: "Index funds and ETFs passively track a market index with very low fees. Historically beat most actively managed funds. +25 points!",
    retryMessage: "Index funds / ETFs passively track an index (like S&P 500) with low fees.",
    category: "Long-Term Investing",
  },
  {
    id: "etf-definition",
    question: "What is an ETF?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "A savings account with higher interest" },
      { id: "B", text: "An electronic transfer fee" },
      { id: "C", text: "Exchange-Traded Fund — a basket of assets traded like a stock" },
      { id: "D", text: "A government emergency fund" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "C",
    reward: 25,
    successMessage: "ETF = basket of assets (stocks, bonds, commodities) tradeable like a single stock. Combines diversification with flexibility. +25 points!",
    retryMessage: "ETF = Exchange-Traded Fund. A basket of assets you can buy/sell like a single stock.",
    category: "Long-Term Investing",
  },
  {
    id: "time-in-market",
    question: "Studies show that for long-term investors, which strategy tends to outperform?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "Timing the market (buy low, sell high perfectly)" },
      { id: "B", text: "Staying invested consistently over time ('time in the market')" },
      { id: "C", text: "Selling when the market drops 10%" },
      { id: "D", text: "Investing only in gold" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "B",
    reward: 30,
    successMessage: "'Time in the market beats timing the market' — missing just 10 best days in 20 years can cut returns in half. +30 points!",
    retryMessage: "Time in market beats timing the market. Consistent, patient investing outperforms most active strategies.",
    category: "Long-Term Investing",
  },

  // ── Retirement ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  {
    id: "retirement-purpose",
    question: "What is the primary purpose of a retirement account?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "To pay for vacations" },
      { id: "B", text: "To replace income when you stop working, using decades of compounding" },
      { id: "C", text: "To speculate on high-risk assets" },
      { id: "D", text: "To store emergency cash" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "B",
    reward: 25,
    successMessage: "Retirement accounts leverage decades of compounding. Starting at 25 vs 35 can mean 2× the final balance. +25 points!",
    retryMessage: "Retirement accounts are long-term compounding vehicles. Time is the biggest asset — start early.",
    category: "Retirement",
  },
  {
    id: "retirement-early-start",
    question: "If you invest $200/month at 7% annual return starting at age 25, approximately how much will you have at 65?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "~$96,000" },
      { id: "B", text: "~$240,000" },
      { id: "C", text: "~$525,000" },
      { id: "D", text: "~$1,200,000" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "C",
    reward: 35,
    successMessage: "~$525,000 from just $200/month! That's 40 years of compounding. Starting at 45 would require ~$800/month for the same result. +35 points!",
    retryMessage: "40 years of $200/month at 7% = ~$525,000. The power of time and compounding is extraordinary.",
    category: "Retirement",
  },

  // ── Poland & Financial Literacy (OECD/INFE) ──────────────────────────────
  {
    id: "poland-compound-gap",
    question: "According to OECD data, what percentage of Poles correctly understand how compound interest works?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "About 75%" },
      { id: "B", text: "About 50%" },
      { id: "C", text: "About 33%" },
      { id: "D", text: "About 10%" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "C",
    reward: 30,
    successMessage: "Only ~1 in 3 Poles understands compound interest. This gap leads directly to debt spirals and low pension savings. +30 points!",
    retryMessage: "Only ~33% of Poles correctly understand compound interest — the OECD data confirms this critical knowledge gap.",
    category: "Financial Literacy",
  },
  {
    id: "poland-trust-institutions",
    question: "In 2022, what percentage of Poles trusted financial institutions for savings and investments?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "65%" },
      { id: "B", text: "40%" },
      { id: "C", text: "28%" },
      { id: "D", text: "15%" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "D",
    reward: 25,
    successMessage: "Only 15% of Poles trusted financial institutions in 2022 — and it bottomed at just 6% in 2021. Trust is the biggest barrier. +25 points!",
    retryMessage: "Only 15% of Poles trusted financial institutions in 2022. The 2021 low was just 6% — a profound trust deficit.",
    category: "Financial Literacy",
  },
  {
    id: "poland-oecd-score",
    question: "What did Poland score on the OECD Financial Competency index?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "19 out of 21" },
      { id: "B", text: "13 out of 21" },
      { id: "C", text: "7 out of 21" },
      { id: "D", text: "21 out of 21" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "B",
    reward: 25,
    successMessage: "Poland scored 13/21 — middle of the pack. The missing 8 points represent lost wealth opportunities for millions of people. +25 points!",
    retryMessage: "Poland scored 13/21 on the OECD Financial Competency index. The gap to maximum represents real lost savings.",
    category: "Financial Literacy",
  },
  {
    id: "poland-ppk-participation",
    question: "What percentage of employees in large Polish firms participate in the voluntary PPK/PPE pension scheme?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "85%" },
      { id: "B", text: "68%" },
      { id: "C", text: "47%" },
      { id: "D", text: "12%" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "C",
    reward: 30,
    successMessage: "Only 47% participate in PPK/PPE — largely because people don't understand compound interest and long-term benefit. +30 points!",
    retryMessage: "Only 47% of employees in large Polish firms use voluntary PPK/PPE schemes — a direct consequence of compound interest illiteracy.",
    category: "Financial Literacy",
  },
  {
    id: "financial-wellbeing-components",
    question: "Financial well-being is measured by three components. Which set is correct?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "Income, spending, borrowing" },
      { id: "B", text: "Control, safety net, future goals" },
      { id: "C", text: "Savings rate, credit score, net worth" },
      { id: "D", text: "Insurance, pension, property" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "B",
    reward: 25,
    successMessage: "Control (daily expenses), Safety Net (emergency cushion), Future Goals (retirement). Master all three to achieve real financial well-being. +25 points!",
    retryMessage: "Financial well-being = Control over daily expenses + Safety Net (poduszka finansowa) + Future Goals like retirement.",
    category: "Financial Literacy",
  },
  {
    id: "financial-resilience",
    question: "How is 'financial resilience' defined by Poland's National Financial Education Strategy?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "Having over $1 million saved" },
      { id: "B", text: "Never borrowing any money" },
      { id: "C", text: "The ability to absorb financial shocks and recover from a difficult material situation" },
      { id: "D", text: "Owning property and having no debt" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "C",
    reward: 30,
    successMessage: "Financial resilience = surviving shocks and bouncing back. It's not about wealth — it's about preparedness. +30 points!",
    retryMessage: "Resilience = ability to deal with adverse financial shocks and recover. It's about preparedness, not wealth level.",
    category: "Financial Literacy",
  },
  {
    id: "debt-spiral-cause",
    question: "What is the primary financial literacy gap that leads to 'debt spirals'?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "Not knowing how to use a credit card" },
      { id: "B", text: "Not understanding compound interest — debt grows faster than expected" },
      { id: "C", text: "Not having a bank account" },
      { id: "D", text: "Spending too much on food" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "B",
    reward: 35,
    successMessage: "Debt spirals happen when people don't realize how fast interest compounds on their loans — the debt grows faster than they can pay. +35 points!",
    retryMessage: "Debt spirals are caused by not understanding compound interest — people underestimate how fast unpaid interest accumulates.",
    category: "Financial Literacy",
  },

  // ── Family Financial Plan ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  {
    id: "insurance-purpose",
    question: "What is the main purpose of life insurance?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "To get rich when someone dies" },
      { id: "B", text: "To replace income for dependents if the primary earner dies" },
      { id: "C", text: "To save on taxes" },
      { id: "D", text: "To invest in the stock market safely" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "B",
    reward: 25,
    successMessage: "Life insurance = income protection for your dependents. If you have people depending on your earnings, you need it. +25 points!",
    retryMessage: "Life insurance protects dependents by replacing the primary earner's income if they die prematurely.",
    category: "Family Financial Plan",
  },
  {
    id: "joint-finances",
    question: "What is the recommended approach to finances for couples?",
    answers: [
      { id: "A", text: "One partner handles all finances, the other doesn't need to know" },
      { id: "B", text: "Both partners should understand the full financial picture and plan together" },
      { id: "C", text: "Keep all finances 100% separate — never share anything" },
      { id: "D", text: "Whoever earns more controls all decisions" },
    ],
    correctAnswer: "B",
    reward: 20,
    successMessage: "Both partners understanding the full financial picture reduces conflict and improves outcomes. +20 points!",
    retryMessage: "Financial transparency and joint planning between partners leads to better decisions and fewer conflicts.",
    category: "Family Financial Plan",
  },
  {
    id: "teaching-kids-money",
